overall.summary: Numbers reproduce, but the not-in-a-family part is said to lower the chance for everyone when it acts only on people not in a family; the capital-gains hypothesis only restates its formula, and the missing-occupation hypothesis is worded causally.

findings.statement: Not reporting an occupation pushes people into a low income; this part captures that effect
findings.evidence: causal overclaim: the evidence shows only that the model predicts a higher chance (62% -> 80%) for a missing occupation (observed 90.7% low income among the 2197); it says nothing about what not reporting does to income
